To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the plasticity of individual leaf area expansion in Arabidopsis is mainly determined by the plasticity of the duration of leaf expansion, which compensates for the decrease in the rate of expansion; that this dynamic plasticity is not detectable by final measurements; and that, in all accessions, moderate water deficits have opposite effects on cell area and cell number.

1) the variability in the plastic response of leaf expansion to water deficit is mostly due to the variability in the rate and duration dynamics of leaf expansion, and 2) the variability in these two dynamics is due to the variability of the underlying cellular and morphogenetic processes, namely the number and size of epidermal cells.

the genetic variability in the plastic response of leaf area expansion to soil water deficit is mainly due to the genetic variability of the duration of leaf expansion, that this variability is not detectable at the cellular level and that the plasticity in the duration of leaf growth is a consequence of the compensation between the opposite effects of water deficit on the rate and the duration of leaf area expansion.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the plasticity to soil water deficits at the whole plant level, and the dissection of the plasticity at the level of individual leaf growth dynamics and cellular variables.
the plasticity of the rate and duration variables of leaf expansion, and the cellular processes involved, and the genetic variability of these processes.

a novel approach for the study of plant plasticity, which is based on the dissection of the phenotypic response of plants to environmental factors into its underlying variables, in order to identify the invisible processes that are at play.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the plasticity in leaf expansion is the result of a combination of the dynamic plasticity in leaf area expansion rate and duration and the cellular plasticity in cell number and cell area.
the plasticity to water deficit is mainly due to a plasticity of leaf expansion rate and duration and that this dynamic plasticity is not detectable by final measurements.

the plasticity in the final leaf size in response to water deficits is due to the compensation between the opposing effects of water deficit on the rate and the duration of individual leaf expansion, which is in turn due to the opposing effects of the deficit on epidermal cell size and number.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

plasticity to soil water deficits in Arabidopsis is mainly due to the dynamic plasticity of the rate and duration leaf expansion and that it is not due to changes in epidermal cell area and cell number.

the variability in the plastic response to water deficit in leaf area expansion in Arabidopsis accessions is mainly due to differences in the rate and duration variables, and that the cellular variables are not sufficient to explain this variability.
plasticity to water deficit is mainly due to dynamic changes and that the compensation between the rate and duration is an important component of this dynamic.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the plasticity of a trait can be dissected into underlying variables that can be used to better understand the mechanisms underlying the plasticity and to better predict how the plasticity of one trait can be linked to that of others.
plasticity to soil water stress is not a simple trait.
the plasticity of a trait can be hidden by the compensation between its underlying dynamic and cellular variables, and thus the use of final measurements can lead to erroneous interpretations.
